title: Sedgwick County CO well depth and costs
meta_description: Sedgwick County wells have a 100 ft median depth and 50 gpm median yield. See typical drilling costs and what to expect for a new well here.
h1: Water wells in Sedgwick County, Colorado
intro_html:
Sedgwick County sits on High Plains alluvium and sedimentary rock, with a mix of domestic, stock, and irrigation wells. County records show 2,264 permitted wells, so there is a decent track record to look at before you buy or drill.

Below is how deep wells actually go here, how much water they tend to produce, what the water table looks like, and what a new well is likely to cost in this part of Colorado.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Sedgwick County
sections.html:
For Sedgwick County as a whole, the median well depth is about 100 feet, with the middle half running from roughly 57 to 320 feet. That lines up with what you’d expect in the plains, where some folks hit shallow alluvial water and others have to go deeper into bedrock.

About 47% of wells are under 100 feet, another 23% are 100–300 feet, and 30% are 300–600 feet. The 90th percentile depth is 380 feet, and the deepest well on record goes down to 3,500 feet, so there are a few very deep completions in the dataset.

Practically, a driller’s bid will often bracket that 57–320 foot middle range, with a clear per-foot price if they have to chase water deeper.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
On paper, Sedgwick County looks strong on production. The median reported pump yield is about 50 gpm, and the middle half of tested wells ranges from roughly 15 to 900 gpm. That wide spread reflects the mix of domestic, stock, and heavier irrigation wells.

Only 2% of tested wells fall in the 1–5 gpm range, and 14% are 5–15 gpm. A full 83% come in above 15 gpm, which is more than enough for typical exempt household use and small-scale stock watering when the well is permitted and constructed correctly.

Keep in mind only 302 wells report a pump test, so these numbers don’t cover every well, but they do give a good sense that truly low-yield completions are uncommon in this county’s records.

sections.heading: Water table depth and longer-term trend
sections.html:
Static water level measurements give a sense of where the water table sits. Across Sedgwick County, the median depth to water is about 40 feet, with the middle half between roughly 18 and 216 feet below ground surface. That’s a wide band, but it matches the variety of alluvial and bedrock settings.

Looking at medians by decade, the water level was around 218 feet in the 1970s, then much shallower at about 39 feet in the 2010s, and about 52 feet so far in the 2020s. That suggests conditions are substantially better than in the 1970s dataset, with some recent variability.

For a specific parcel, your best information will be nearby well logs and any recent static level measurements within the same aquifer zone.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and for what uses
sections.html:
Sedgwick County has a long history of well development. Permits ramped up from 142 in the 1950s to peaks of 288 in the 1990s and 299 in the 2000s. There were 205 permits in the 2010s and 97 already in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025, so new wells are still going in.

Use is spread across domestic/household (29%), stock (27%), irrigation (34%), and monitoring (9%). That mix explains the wide range of depths and yields.

Most wells are completed in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers (1,788 wells), with the Ogallala listed on 338 wells and local Alluvial aquifers on 31. The most active drillers in the records are Jim Feighny & Sons, Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc, and Haggard Drilling Inc.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Sedgwick County
sections.html:
The drilling cost model for Sedgwick County assumes alluvium over plains sedimentary rock, with a typical rate of about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 100 foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $3,500–$5,500.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the model puts a finished domestic well in the ballpark of $9,500–$17,500. Deeper completions toward the upper end of the 57–320 foot common range will push you to the higher side of that spread.

Bid the job with a clear per-foot price, plus line items for materials and setup, and make sure the driller is familiar with the Ogallala and local bedrock aquifers used around Julesburg, Sedgwick, and Ovid.

sections.heading: Risks to check: quality, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
From the county data, outright low-yield wells are relatively rare, with 0% of tested wells under 1 gpm and only 2% in the 1–5 gpm band. Still, any new domestic well should get a proper pump test, especially if you plan on irrigation or livestock.

On the water-quality side, there are about 5 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within roughly 10 miles. That does not mean your well is contaminated, but it is a strong reason to order a full lab test panel at closing and recheck every few years.

Also watch your well and septic layout: maintain proper separation distances, and give future building locations, driveways, and irrigation plans some thought before you pick a drill spot.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Sedgwick County well lot
sections.html:
With 2,264 total permits and 1,492 reporting depths, Sedgwick County has enough data that you shouldn’t be guessing. Before you buy a rural parcel, pull logs for nearby wells and compare depths, yields, and static levels, especially in areas transitioning between alluvium and fractured bedrock.

If the parcel already has a well, confirm the permitted use (domestic, stock, irrigation, or monitoring) and verify construction details and any pump test data. For a vacant lot, budget using the 57–320 foot “middle half” depth range, and make sure your lender is comfortable with that spread.

Areas around Julesburg, Ovid, and Sedgwick each have their own patterns, so look locally rather than just at county-wide medians when you make a drilling or purchase decision.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Sedgwick County, Colorado?
faq.a: Across Sedgwick County, the median well depth is about 100 feet, with the middle half of wells between roughly 57 and 320 feet deep. About 47% of wells are under 100 feet, 23% run 100–300 feet, and 30% fall in the 300–600 foot band. The 90th percentile depth is around 380 feet, and the deepest recorded well in the county reaches about 3,500 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Sedgwick County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported production is generally strong. The median tested yield is about 50 gpm, with the middle half of wells between roughly 15 and 900 gpm. In the records, 0% of tested wells are under 1 gpm, 2% are 1–5 gpm, 14% are 5–15 gpm, and 83% produce more than 15 gpm. Only 302 wells report a pump test, but those suggest low-yield completions are not common.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Sedgwick County?
faq.a: The drilling cost model for Sedgwick County uses a rate of about $35–$55 per foot in local alluvium and sedimentary rock. At the county’s 100 foot median depth, that puts the bare hole at roughly $3,500–$5,500. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical typically totals around $9,500–$17,500, depending on depth and equipment choices.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sedgwick County, Colorado?
faq.a: County records don’t give a single safety rating, but there are about 5 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within roughly 10 miles. That makes water testing important. For any existing or new well, budget for a full lab water test at purchase and repeat testing every few years, especially if you are near known industrial or agricultural areas.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels in Sedgwick County going down?
faq.a: The limited static water level data show a mixed picture. Median depth to water was about 218 feet in the 1970s dataset, then much shallower at roughly 39 feet in the 2010s, and about 52 feet so far in the 2020s. Overall, that suggests water levels are significantly shallower than in the 1970s records but have shown some variability in recent years. Check nearby, recent measurements for a specific property.
